 Wet Leg vs Dry Leg: 6 Essential Steps for Accurate DP Level

 A closed vessel pushes its vapour pressure onto both sides of a DP transmitter, and the way you connect the low side decides whether that pressure cancels cleanly. Choosing between a dry or filled reference line, and ranging it correctly, is the heart of reliable DP level.

 
 Dry Leg 
 Filled Reference Leg 
 Zero Elevation 
 LRV and URV 
 




 A wet leg is a reference line filled with a stable liquid that connects the vessel top to the low side of a DP level transmitter. It removes condensation errors but needs zero elevation, careful fill fluid choice and a correct LRV and URV calculation.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a wet leg and a dry leg work in DP level measurement, when to use each one and how to calculate the LRV and URV.


 
 
 
 What Is a Wet Leg in DP Level Measurement?


 A wet leg is the low pressure impulse line of a closed tank DP level transmitter, deliberately kept full of liquid from the upper vessel tap down to the transmitter. A dry leg is the same line kept full of gas or vapour, as introduced in DP transmitter level measurement .


 In a closed vessel, the gas pressure above the liquid acts on both taps. Connecting the upper tap to the low side of a differential pressure transmitter subtracts that pressure, so only the liquid head remains.


 
 
 Image credit: Control Global . Illustration courtesy of Control Global, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 Control Global, in an article by contributing editor Paul Miller, explains that dry legs suit non condensing vapour spaces while filled reference legs handle vapours that may condense. The same article quotes an instrumentation specialist who calls DP perhaps the most simple and reliable technology for measuring level as well as flow.


 Do You Know?
 The reading of a filled reference line runs backwards compared with a dry leg. The DP is most negative when the tank is empty and rises toward zero as the tank fills.



 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 How a Dry Leg Works


 In a dry leg, the high side senses vapour pressure plus liquid head while the low side senses vapour pressure alone. The two vapour pressures cancel, so DP equals level times specific gravity, plus any head below the lower tap.


 The method works only while the line stays dry. CANTEACH training notes from the CANDU nuclear industry explain that condensable vapour such as steam forms condensate in the low side line, which then needs a knock out pot and frequent draining, much like a condensate pot in steam applications .


 Quick Tip
 On a dry leg, slope the line continuously back toward the vessel so any condensate drains away by itself. A single sag can trap liquid and shift the zero without warning.



 How a Wet Leg Works


 In this arrangement, the low side line is filled completely with liquid, either the condensed process vapour or a separate seal fluid. Its head is constant, so it can be subtracted during ranging, which is called zero elevation in zero elevation and zero suppression .


 
 Vapour Space Same pressure acts on both taps

 Upper Tap Connects to a seal or condensing pot

 Filled Line Constant liquid column to the low side

 Lower Tap Process liquid to the high side

 DP Output Level head minus fixed leg head

 Ranging LRV negative, URV near zero




 Because the leg head is larger than the level head, the DP stays negative across the range. Steam drums use this arrangement, as described in boiler drum level control , because steam condenses and keeps the leg naturally full.


 
 73 percent Density of 304 °C drum water vs 38 °C water 

 5 percent Saturated steam density at 1310 psig 

 1 inch Minimum pipe to the condensing pot 

 13 inch False DP from an uncompensated full drum 




 Control Engineering, in an article by Chris Hardy of Cross Company, notes that water at 580 °F, about 304 °C, is only 73 percent as dense as water at 100 °F. He also states that the condensing pot must not be insulated, since insulation stops the condensation that keeps the leg full.


 Wet Leg vs Dry Leg Comparison


 
 
 Feature Dry Leg Wet Leg 

 Low side line contents Gas or vapour Liquid, condensate or seal fluid 

 Vapour type suited Non condensing Condensing, such as steam 

 Ranging Zero suppression or true zero Zero elevation, LRV negative 

 Main error source Condensate collecting in line Leg losing fluid or changing density 

 Maintenance Drain knock out pot Refill and check leg level 

 



 The same choice appears on vessels with remote seals, where a capillary filled with oil acts as a sealed wet leg. Fill fluid choice is covered in fill fluid selection for diaphragm seals , and capillary routing rules appear in capillary tubing in pressure measurements .


 Choosing the Fill Fluid for a Wet Leg


 
 Process Condensate
 Vapour condenses in a pot and keeps the leg full automatically.
 Best for: steam drums, deaerators
 Self filling 

 Glycol Water Mixture
 Lower freezing point for outdoor legs.
 Best for: cold climates, chilled service
 Freeze safe 

 Silicone Oil
 Stable density over a wide temperature range.
 Best for: capillary seals, sealed systems
 Low drift 

 Inert Seal Liquid
 Immiscible liquid that protects the transmitter.
 Best for: corrosive or toxic vapours
 Isolating 




 The fill must not mix with or dissolve into the process, and its specific gravity must stay stable, as explained in what is specific gravity . A seal pot at the top lets you top up the leg and see its level.


 Do You Know?
 If a filled leg slowly loses fluid, the DP rises and the indicated level climbs even though the tank is unchanged. Operators then see a high level that does not exist.
